To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) the direction of the change in the degree of bias due to adjusting for a variable depends on the direction of the dependence of that variable on the confounder; 2) the direction of change is the same for all types of bias (i.e., bias due to confounding, bias due to selection, and bias due to non-compliance); and 3) the direction of bias change is opposite for bias in the causal association and bias in the noncausal association.

(i) adjustment for a common cause of both the exposure and outcome may increase or decrease the degree of bias (i.e., may make the association between the exposure and outcome more or less consistent with the underlying causal model) and may even reverse the sign of the bias, depending on the relative strengths of the associations between the exposure and the outcome and between the exposure and its common cause; and (ii) adjustment for a mediator of the causal effect of an exposure on an outcome may increase or

the direction of change in the bias in a causal effect due to adjustment depends on the direction of the association between the confounder and both the exposure and outcome, and the direction of the causal effect of the confounder on the outcome.
In summary, our research is concerned with
identifying the conditions under which the effect of a covariate is altered by conditioning on other variables.
identifying conditions under which adjustment for a third variable may alter a relationship between two other variables, and with the direction and magnitude of that change.

understanding the consequences of adjusting for a confounder on the bias of an association, and how this bias can be reduced by appropriate adjustment, or how it can be increased by inappropriate adjustment.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

, in general, adjusting for a third (and fourth, etc.) variable may increase, reduce or leave unchanged the bias in estimating the association between two variables, and that the direction of the bias is determined by the nature of the causal relationships among the variables.
, in the absence of confounding, adjusting for a third factor will not alter the bias in the association between two factors, but it may alter the degree of bias when there is confounding.
, in general, the effect of adjustment is to increase, decrease or leave unchanged the bias in an estimate of a causal effect.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the graphical rules are very useful for understanding how to use adjustment to estimate causal effects, but that they are not always sufficient for this purpose.
noncollapsibility is a general phenomenon, but that the consequences for bias in causal effect estimation are often more complex than is commonly assumed.
, in general, adjustment will reduce bias if the third variable is a cause of the first and a consequence of the second.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the direction of bias in an estimated causal effect of one exposure on another can be predicted from the sign of the partial correlation between the exposure and outcome, conditional on the confounders, and from the sign of partial correlation between the confounders themselves.
graphical models can be used to identify the conditions under which adjusting for a variable will alter the association between two others and the direction of that change.
the effects of adjustment can be understood by considering the structure of the underlying causal diagram.
